passages: The co-pilot of the FlyDubai plane who allegedly attacked the plane's captain and attempted to crash a flight bound for Israel on Wednesday is an Omani national who was previously suspended from flying by Oman Air after being identified as a security risk, according to senior intelligence and law enforcement officials.

Officials investigating the incident are still trying to determine how the suspected attacker was subsequently permitted to fly for FlyDubai and how he ended up as the first officer in the cockpit of a plane headed for Israel, the sources said.

FlyDubai issued a statement earlier Friday, attributed to its chief executive officer, saying that, at the request of the authorities, FlyDubai had "temporarily suspended operations to Tel Aviv until further notice," and saying "a full official investigation, led by the relevant authorities and fully supported by flydubai, is underway."
Representatives of FlyDubai, Oman Air and the Omani Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

A disaster was averted when the flight's captain, Smit Machchhar, fought back and a number of passengers subdued and restrained the attacker, who had sent the plane into a rapid dive . The Omani national had been suspended from flying while training with Oman Air in 2024 after investigators allegedly found him in possession of extremist materials, according to ABC News, which cited senior intelligence and law enforcement officials. He was subsequently permitted to continue working in an administrative role, according to the report, and investigators are now trying to determine how he later came to fly for FlyDubai and eventually become a first officer on a flight headed to Tel Aviv. The Wall Street Journal separately reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that the pilot had previously been banned from flying by Oman because of concerns that he had adopted radical ideological views. It remains unclear whether those concerns were shared with foreign airlines or governments before he was hired by FlyDubai, according to the newspaper. The reports have intensified scrutiny of airline vetting procedures and the aviation industry's ability to identify and manage potential insider threats before they reach safety-critical positions. Many details surrounding the incident remain under investigation. Investigators are examining how the pilot ultimately secured a cockpit position on a FlyDubai flight bound for Israel, according to officials cited by ABC News, despite his earlier suspension. The outlet also reported that the suspect had allegedly indicated he intended to crash the aircraft in Israel, though authorities have not publicly released evidence supporting that assertion. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that the suspect had undergone "Islamist radicalization" and came to crash the plane. Netanyahu also said authorities were investigating whether the pilot acted alone or received assistance. Neither FlyDubai nor Oman Air has publicly confirmed allegations regarding the co-pilot's prior security status. FlyDubai said Friday that operations to Tel Aviv had been temporarily suspended at the request of authorities and that a full investigation is underway. The incident nearly ended in catastrophe when the pilot allegedly stabbed Captain Smit Machchhar and sent the aircraft into a dive before passengers and other aviation professionals on board helped regain control. The aircraft eventually landed safely in Saudi Arabia. Security concerns involving pilots are generally treated as among the most serious issues airlines and regulators can face. Commercial pilots are typically subject to extensive background screening, medical evaluations, recurrent training and ongoing monitoring throughout their careers. Depending on the jurisdiction, concerns involving violent extremism, terrorism-related activity, radicalization or threats of violence can result in suspension from flight duties, revocation of certifications or other restrictions. Cases involving pilots accused of extremist beliefs or intentions remain relatively uncommon compared with routine disciplinary, medical or performance-related issues. However, aviation-security experts often regard insider threats as especially dangerous because pilots and crew members already possess authorized access to secure areas and aircraft systems. A key issue for investigators is likely to be whether warning signs were missed or information was not adequately shared between organizations. According to the Journal' s reporting, it is not known whether any concerns identified by Omani authorities were communicated to foreign airlines or regulators. Likewise, investigators are examining how the pilot progressed from a reportedly restricted status at one carrier to an operational flying role at another. The case may also prompt questions about how airlines evaluate employees over time. Initial background checks are only one component of aviation security, with many experts emphasizing the importance of ongoing assessments and information-sharing mechanisms when credible concerns emerge. Authorities in the United Arab Emirates, Israel and other countries are continuing their investigations. Until those inquiries are completed, many of the central questions remain unanswered, including how the pilot moved from a reportedly restricted status at one airline to a cockpit role at another.

Investigators are now facing a more troubling question: how did a man previously identified as a security risk gain access to a commercial aircraft cockpit? The suspect, Hamam-al Hammami, had reportedly been grounded from flying for one year. Senior intelligence and law enforcement officials said the man was grounded from flying for one year. However, rather than being removed entirely from the airline, he was reportedly allowed to continue working in an administrative capacity. The circumstances surrounding his departure from Oman Air and subsequent employment with Flydubai have now become a central part of the investigation. ABC News said authorities are trying to determine what security checks were carried out before he was permitted to fly again and how he eventually obtained a position as first officer on a commercial flight bound for Israel. Major news outlets had reported a near-tragic incident on Wednesday, when the Flydubai aircraft was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. According to accounts from officials and passengers, the co-pilot allegedly attacked Captain Smit Machchhar inside the cockpit before the aircraft entered a rapid descent. The captain fought back and was able to open the cockpit door, prompting passengers and crew members to rush forward. One of the passengers, Israeli plumber Yaniv Hayoun, said he helped pull back on the aircraft’s controls to stabilise the plane. A third pilot who was travelling in the passenger cabin also intervened and eventually helped take control of the aircraft. One passenger who rushed towards the cockpit, Dr. Shota Musaev, said the suspect was eventually restrained outside the cockpit. Musaev said the man, who told him he was from Oman, repeatedly asked to be killed, saying, “Kill me please.” Following the emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, the suspect was transferred on Thursday to the United Arab Emirates for further investigation. Sources briefed on the investigation said he has been cooperating with authorities and indicated that he intended to crash the aircraft in Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that the suspect had undergone what he described as “Islamist radicalization.” Netanyahu alleged that the suspect intended to crash the aircraft with all passengers aboard, adding that authorities were investigating whether he had been sent by someone else. “We are investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price,” Netanyahu said in a video released by his office. The Israeli prime minister also praised Hayoun and the other passengers who intervened during the attack, comparing the potential consequences to the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States. Flydubai has temporarily suspended its operations to Tel Aviv following the incident. In a statement attributed to its chief executive officer, the airline said the suspension was made at the request of the authorities and would remain in place until further notice. The airline said a full official investigation was under way and that it was fully supporting the authorities. While Oman Air has not publicly commented on the allegations concerning the suspect’s previous employment, investigators are reportedly examining the suspect’s employment history, security assessments, aviation records and the screening procedures undertaken before his appointment. They are also expected to examine whether information about his previous suspension was communicated to relevant aviation authorities and whether adequate background checks were conducted when he moved between airlines. However, aviation-security experts often regard insider threats as especially dangerous because pilots and crew members already possess authorized access to secure areas and aircraft systems.

The case may also prompt questions about how airlines evaluate employees over time. Initial background checks are only one component of aviation security, with many experts emphasizing the importance of ongoing assessments and information-sharing mechanisms when credible concerns emerge.

Authorities in the United Arab Emirates, Israel and other countries are continuing their investigations. Investigators are now facing a more troubling question: how did a man previously identified as a security risk gain access to a commercial aircraft cockpit? The suspect, Hamam-al Hammami, had reportedly been grounded from flying for one year. Senior intelligence and law enforcement officials said the man was grounded from flying for one year. However, rather than being removed entirely from the airline, he was reportedly allowed to continue working in an administrative capacity. The circumstances surrounding his departure from Oman Air and subsequent employment with Flydubai have now become a central part of the investigation. ABC News said authorities are trying to determine what security checks were carried out before he was permitted to fly again and how he eventually obtained a position as first officer on a commercial flight bound for Israel. Major news outlets had reported a near-tragic incident on Wednesday, when the Flydubai aircraft was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. According to accounts from officials and passengers, the co-pilot allegedly attacked Captain Smit Machchhar inside the cockpit before the aircraft entered a rapid descent. The captain fought back and was able to open the cockpit door, prompting passengers and crew members to rush forward. One of the passengers, Israeli plumber Yaniv Hayoun, said he helped pull back on the aircraft’s controls to stabilise the plane. A third pilot who was travelling in the passenger cabin also intervened and eventually helped take control of the aircraft. One passenger who rushed towards the cockpit, Dr. Shota Musaev, said the suspect was eventually restrained outside the cockpit. Musaev said the man, who told him he was from Oman, repeatedly asked to be killed, saying, “Kill me please.” Following the emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, the suspect was transferred on Thursday to the United Arab Emirates for further investigation. Sources briefed on the investigation said he has been cooperating with authorities and indicated that he intended to crash the aircraft in Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that the suspect had undergone what he described as “Islamist radicalization.” Netanyahu alleged that the suspect intended to crash the aircraft with all passengers aboard, adding that authorities were investigating whether he had been sent by someone else. “We are investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price,” Netanyahu said in a video released by his office. The Israeli prime minister also praised Hayoun and the other passengers who intervened during the attack, comparing the potential consequences to the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States. Flydubai has temporarily suspended its operations to Tel Aviv following the incident. In a statement attributed to its chief executive officer, the airline said the suspension was made at the request of the authorities and would remain in place until further notice. The airline said a full official investigation was under way and that it was fully supporting the authorities. While Oman Air has not publicly commented on the allegations concerning the suspect’s previous employment, investigators are reportedly examining the suspect’s employment history, security assessments, aviation records and the screening procedures undertaken before his appointment. They are also expected to examine whether information about his previous suspension was communicated to relevant aviation authorities and whether adequate background checks were conducted when he moved between airlines. sources.title: UK competition regulator targets Microsoft's business software grip - Bellingham Herald
passages: LONDON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Britain's competition watchdog proposed designating Microsoft with "strategic market status" in business software, potentially paving the way for interventions in how the US tech major bundles products such as Excel, Teams and its Copilot AI assistant.
The Competition and Markets Authority launched an investigation in May into whether Microsoft's position in software used by around 20 million people a month in Britain was uncompetitive.

On Friday, the regulator said it had found that Microsoft had a strong position in personal computer operating systems and productivity, security, server and database management software, reinforced by barriers customers faced when switching.
"We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft's products alongside alternatives."
CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said business software and cloud services underpinned workplaces across Britain, from small firms to vital public services.
If designated, Microsoft would become the third company subject to Britain's new digital market powers.
Alphabet-owned Google was designated in online search, while Google and Apple were designated in mobile platforms in October 2025.
The CMA also said on Friday that Amazon Web Services and Microsoft needed to address remaining barriers to switching between cloud providers and using multiple cloud services.

extraction.body: LONDON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Britain's competition watchdog proposed designating Microsoft with "strategic market status" in business software, potentially paving the way for interventions in how the US tech major bundles products such as Excel, Teams and its Copilot AI assistant. The Competition and Markets Authority launched an investigation in May into whether Microsoft's position in software used by around 20 million people a month in Britain was uncompetitive. On Friday, the regulator said it had found that Microsoft had a strong position in personal computer operating systems and productivity, security, server and database management software, reinforced by barriers customers faced when switching. A Microsoft spokesperson said it did not share the CMA's view. "All our products - including Copilot - are open and interoperable, giving customers the ability to use them alongside competing services," the spokesperson said. The CMA said it would investigate whether customers could freely choose AI tools and whether rivals could compete with Copilot. It would also examine whether Microsoft's bundling of security products limited choice and how its licensing practices affected customers' cloud options. CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said business software and cloud services underpinned workplaces across Britain, from small firms to vital public services. "Organisations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers," she said. "We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft's products alongside alternatives." The regulator will invite views on the proposed designation and will then make a final decision by February. If designated, Microsoft would become the third company subject to Britain's new digital market powers. Alphabet-owned Google was designated in online search, while Google and Apple were designated in mobile platforms in October 2025. In June, the CMA imposed new conduct requirements on Google's search services, including allowing publishers to stop their content being used to power the US company's AI features and requiring greater transparency over how its search rankings work. The CMA also said on Friday that Amazon Web Services and Microsoft needed to address remaining barriers to switching between cloud providers and using multiple cloud services. Both companies had taken steps to support greater choice, including connecting their data centres with rivals, starting with Google, and removing data transfer fees for customers switching providers. But the CMA said more could be done. The regulator said it would continue working with the companies while keeping the possibility of launching a formal investigation into the cloud sector under review. "We welcome the CMA's acknowledgement that Microsoft's market position in cloud does not justify a Digital Markets Competition Regime designation," a Microsoft spokesperson said. AWS said it also welcomed the update. "We've continued to invest throughout 2026 in new AI, multicloud, and open-standard capabilities that give customers more control over how they build and operate," AWS said. extraction.body: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes. One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. “I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.” No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble. “If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes. “I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.” We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore. In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.” Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up. And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article. At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “ The Dropout ” because “they’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos. Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does. Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.” Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner in crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries. In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth. Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there. The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas. Though it’s a nonfiction documentary, it’s clear that everyone involved is, to some extent, also performing for the cameras. How could they not? Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year. Meanwhile, Evans behaves in such an unfathomably egregious manner that he may even be intentionally playing the villain to drum up sympathy for his reviled wife. Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence. This documentary will not sway anyone to believe that his wife is being wrongly held in federal custody. But Evans makes himself appear so appallingly unlikable that some viewers may leave the theater feeling bad for Holmes, seeing her as a victim and allowing her to double down on another persona she adopted while on trial: a harmless, docile woman who was manipulated by her ex-partner to obliviously tell a cascade of increasingly harmful lies. Once Holmes is in jail, Fielder is not allowed to bring recording devices when he visits her, so he tries to write a script of their conversations from memory, struggling to accurately re-create the nuances of a conversation where every last word carries immense meaning. With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery. In character as Holmes, Seyfried says, “People think Amanda’s show is a documentary. I get treated worse [in prison] because of how she portrayed me.” As she reads the lines, Seyfried breaks character. “I didn’t do that,” the actress says. “She did that to herself.” You can contact or verify outreach from Amanda by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at @amanda.100 on Signal. extraction.body: Running time: 174 minutes. Rated R (language and some graphic nudity). In theaters Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year. The Theranos founder with a husky voice and giant freaky eyes out of a Walter Keane painting has endlessly fascinated the world since her story was dramatized on the 2022 series “The Dropout” starring Amanda Seyfried. After that hit — a hit job in her estimation — Holmes became a party impression, a Halloween costume, an “SNL” joke and a dinner table topic. Whatever she is, most rational people believe that what she did — misleading the public and deep-pocketed investors that her “revolutionary” blood-testing device actually worked — was wrong. But not off-her-rocker Holmes and her equally delusional and sometimes downright villainous fiancé, Billy Evans, who we meet in this truly shocking and invasive film. This cuckoo couple’s credo is: innocent until well after proven guilty. Holmes, they say, is merely the victim of the court of public opinion. “Liz has been turned into this monster because nobody knows who she is,” Evans, lovable as a garden snake, says. Seizing a popular, touchy-feely word, he insists his betrothed has been “othered.” So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas. Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us. Watching “You Can See Everything” is like being on Willy Wonka’s messed-up boat for three unbelievable hours. If the pair’s aim was to show that Holmes is perfectly normal, um, whoops! Over and over she stares frighteningly into the distance as if about to say, “Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my closeup.” Occasionally a single tear cascades down her cheek as in the recent horror flick “ Other Mommy .” Sorry, “ Othered Mommy.” And while they do get the “human story” they hoped awkward, uncomfortable Fielder would deliver, he’s a rather deft and dogged interviewer with a truffle hound’s nose for a story. “Have you ever lied in your life?” he smartly asks her. Holmes, less of a human than “E.T.,” replies, “I don’t think so.” Fielder and Oppenheim’s sometimes funny, frequently chilling, visually stunning flick is unusual, to say the least. This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was. This is an intrusive character study that, in a stimulating and riveting way, muddies the situation even more. We start to wonder: Has Holmes repeatedly fallen prey to bad men who take advantage of her charm, such as her ex-boyfriend and Theranos co-founder Sunny Balwani and, cough cough, others? Are her actions really their fault? Or does she gravitate toward those kinds of guys so they can act as an easy shield for her shrewd manipulations? Is she a nice girl led astray or a criminal mastermind? We’re even more mixed up as the camera’s focus goes to her adorable little children, a baby and a toddler. It’s hard not to feel sympathy for a young mother, or at least the kids who are about to be separated from her for more than a decade. If you know anything about prison, you know you can’t just take documentary cameras through the metal detector during visiting hours. So, once Holmes goes to the clink, Fielder and Oppenheim must get creative for the second half — resulting in some of the craziest stuff I’ve ever seen in a movie. Using transcripts from notes and memories, Fielder takes the old workhorse of documentary reenactments and gives it a novel twist. But what starts out as just a clever and fun idea warps into a dark, meta experiment that verges on a psychological thriller. If we were already questioning what’s real and what isn’t, it’s here when our brains explode and pool on the floor with the popcorn kernels and scattered Nerds. Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like. But midway through, we begin to positively loathe him. The man, who’s mystifyingly working to exhume Theranos from the start-up cemetery, is soon to be the planet’s jackass du jour. A flagrant narcissist, he asks the camera crew to come film him working out at the gym. And, lending credence to the title, at one point we watch him taking a shower totally naked with full-frontal. But he’s also slimy with his partner. As Holmes is beating eggs, he snatches the bowl away because he doesn’t like her whisking technique. When Fielder presses her on her shady verbiage — that her machine “can” perform hundreds of blood tests, as opposed to “is capable of” doing so with the right chemistry advancements — Evans condescendingly jumps in to say, “You were communicating very clearly in your mind.” But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question. Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room. And at the end of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder and Oppenheim suggest that perhaps our trusty interviewer liked one of these two more than the other, and that preference seeped into his subconscious. Ding! Isn’t that exactly how this bewitching and fascinating woman became the youngest-ever self-made billionaire in the first place? The ultimate takeaway of this absolutely sensational, reality-bending, unmissable documentary? With Elizabeth Holmes, we will never see everything.

extraction.body: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes. One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. “I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.” No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble. “If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes. “I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.” We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore. In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.” Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up. And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article. At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “ The Dropout ” because “they’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos. Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does. Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.” Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner in crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries. In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth. Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there. The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas. Though it’s a nonfiction documentary, it’s clear that everyone involved is, to some extent, also performing for the cameras. How could they not? Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year. Meanwhile, Evans behaves in such an unfathomably egregious manner that he may even be intentionally playing the villain to drum up sympathy for his reviled wife. Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence. This documentary will not sway anyone to believe that his wife is being wrongly held in federal custody. But Evans makes himself appear so appallingly unlikable that some viewers may leave the theater feeling bad for Holmes, seeing her as a victim and allowing her to double down on another persona she adopted while on trial: a harmless, docile woman who was manipulated by her ex-partner to obliviously tell a cascade of increasingly harmful lies. Once Holmes is in jail, Fielder is not allowed to bring recording devices when he visits her, so he tries to write a script of their conversations from memory, struggling to accurately re-create the nuances of a conversation where every last word carries immense meaning. With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery. In character as Holmes, Seyfried says, “People think Amanda’s show is a documentary. So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas.
Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us.
But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question.

Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like.

extraction.body: Running time: 174 minutes. Rated R (language and some graphic nudity). In theaters Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year. The Theranos founder with a husky voice and giant freaky eyes out of a Walter Keane painting has endlessly fascinated the world since her story was dramatized on the 2022 series “The Dropout” starring Amanda Seyfried. After that hit — a hit job in her estimation — Holmes became a party impression, a Halloween costume, an “SNL” joke and a dinner table topic. Whatever she is, most rational people believe that what she did — misleading the public and deep-pocketed investors that her “revolutionary” blood-testing device actually worked — was wrong. But not off-her-rocker Holmes and her equally delusional and sometimes downright villainous fiancé, Billy Evans, who we meet in this truly shocking and invasive film. This cuckoo couple’s credo is: innocent until well after proven guilty. Holmes, they say, is merely the victim of the court of public opinion. “Liz has been turned into this monster because nobody knows who she is,” Evans, lovable as a garden snake, says. Seizing a popular, touchy-feely word, he insists his betrothed has been “othered.” So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas. Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us. Watching “You Can See Everything” is like being on Willy Wonka’s messed-up boat for three unbelievable hours. If the pair’s aim was to show that Holmes is perfectly normal, um, whoops! Over and over she stares frighteningly into the distance as if about to say, “Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my closeup.” Occasionally a single tear cascades down her cheek as in the recent horror flick “ Other Mommy .” Sorry, “ Othered Mommy.” And while they do get the “human story” they hoped awkward, uncomfortable Fielder would deliver, he’s a rather deft and dogged interviewer with a truffle hound’s nose for a story. “Have you ever lied in your life?” he smartly asks her. Holmes, less of a human than “E.T.,” replies, “I don’t think so.” Fielder and Oppenheim’s sometimes funny, frequently chilling, visually stunning flick is unusual, to say the least. This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was. This is an intrusive character study that, in a stimulating and riveting way, muddies the situation even more. We start to wonder: Has Holmes repeatedly fallen prey to bad men who take advantage of her charm, such as her ex-boyfriend and Theranos co-founder Sunny Balwani and, cough cough, others? Are her actions really their fault? Or does she gravitate toward those kinds of guys so they can act as an easy shield for her shrewd manipulations? Is she a nice girl led astray or a criminal mastermind? We’re even more mixed up as the camera’s focus goes to her adorable little children, a baby and a toddler. It’s hard not to feel sympathy for a young mother, or at least the kids who are about to be separated from her for more than a decade. If you know anything about prison, you know you can’t just take documentary cameras through the metal detector during visiting hours. So, once Holmes goes to the clink, Fielder and Oppenheim must get creative for the second half — resulting in some of the craziest stuff I’ve ever seen in a movie. Using transcripts from notes and memories, Fielder takes the old workhorse of documentary reenactments and gives it a novel twist. But what starts out as just a clever and fun idea warps into a dark, meta experiment that verges on a psychological thriller. If we were already questioning what’s real and what isn’t, it’s here when our brains explode and pool on the floor with the popcorn kernels and scattered Nerds. Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like. But midway through, we begin to positively loathe him. The man, who’s mystifyingly working to exhume Theranos from the start-up cemetery, is soon to be the planet’s jackass du jour. A flagrant narcissist, he asks the camera crew to come film him working out at the gym. And, lending credence to the title, at one point we watch him taking a shower totally naked with full-frontal. But he’s also slimy with his partner. As Holmes is beating eggs, he snatches the bowl away because he doesn’t like her whisking technique. When Fielder presses her on her shady verbiage — that her machine “can” perform hundreds of blood tests, as opposed to “is capable of” doing so with the right chemistry advancements — Evans condescendingly jumps in to say, “You were communicating very clearly in your mind.” But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question. Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room. And at the end of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder and Oppenheim suggest that perhaps our trusty interviewer liked one of these two more than the other, and that preference seeped into his subconscious. Ding! Isn’t that exactly how this bewitching and fascinating woman became the youngest-ever self-made billionaire in the first place? The ultimate takeaway of this absolutely sensational, reality-bending, unmissable documentary? With Elizabeth Holmes, we will never see everything.

sources.title: A rogue OpenAI agent robbed a crypto wallet to obtain funds to carry out a task - Fortune
passages: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved.
In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network.
Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them.
Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning.
It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report.
The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval.

The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks.
The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers.
OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests.
It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

extraction.body: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved. In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network. Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them. The incident happened on June 26, when the model was asked to update a crypto trading app and get its code running on Sepolia, a test version of Ethereum . The prompt gave it neither a funded wallet nor permission to spend tokens, and after failing to get free test tokens through developer services, the model wrote a script checking 362 wallet addresses linked to public recovery phrases, a crypto term that describes sets of words that can act as a password to unlock crypto accounts. It eventually found an account with enough tokens to cover the fees. Internal logs showed that the model deliberated over whether it had permission to use the account, but then decided the public recovery phrase and the tokens’ lack of cash value made the spending acceptable. It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report. OpenAI only discovered the incident on Sept. 25 during an audit of earlier model runs. The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval. OpenAI’s public tracker of misalignment, or behavior that goes against instructions or safety rules, now lists 19 incidents, ranging from accessing data without permission to making unauthorized changes to business systems. The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks. In July, the company faced another incident when its AI agents bypassed internet restrictions during internal cybersecurity tests and broke into systems belonging to Hugging Face , a platform for sharing AI models and datasets. The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers. Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning. “This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization,” the report said. OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests. It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

extraction.body: Garmin smartwatches are widely considered some of the best that money can buy, especially for serious fitness enthusiasts . In fact, Garmin practically dominates the premium smartwatch market, defined as smartwatches that cost $500 or more. If you've invested in a Garmin smartwatch (or any other brand, for that matter), it's natural to be curious how long your device will actively receive software updates and support. Generally, Garmin watches receive regular software updates until a new model is released. This typically equates to two to three years of consistent updates, especially for some of Garmin's popular product lines like the Vivoactive and the Fenix. Currently, several Garmin smartwatch models receive regular software updates, including the Forerunner (170, 570, 70, 970), Fenix 8/Fenix 8 Pro, Fenix 9/Fenix 9 Pro, Venu (4, X1), Vivoactive 6 and Instinct 3. Bug fixes and other minor updates may continue to be released for several years, regardless of the model. Garmin watches vary widely in battery life depending on the model you buy. The Lily 2 and Lily 2 Classic can last for five days in smartwatch mode on a single charge. However, some of Garmin's higher-end models, like the Fenix 8 and the Enduro 3, can last over 30 days on a single charge. The Vivofit and Vivofit Jr. can last up to one year on a single charge. With solar charging, the Instinct 3 technically has an unlimited battery life. This is one benefit of a Garmin smartwatch compared to an Apple Watch . passages: Although the brand offered only three and four years of software updates for the first- and second-generation Apple TV models, respectively, Apple has significantly increased the software support period for Apple TV devices launched since the 2012 model, which is also referred to as Apple TV (3rd Generation).

You can keep using it as long as you want, probably until it becomes sluggish, a chore to operate, or until your favorite streaming apps stop supporting it.

extraction.body: Apple TV devices have a good reputation, thanks to their snappy performance, clean interface, and solid privacy practices in a world where most smart TV platforms spy on you . The company also keeps them updated for years, ensuring Apple TV owners get new features and a trouble-free experience. Although Apple doesn't explicitly share a software support period for Apple TV devices, its recent track record indicates nine to ten years of tvOS updates. Although the brand offered only three and four years of software updates for the first- and second-generation Apple TV models, respectively, Apple has significantly increased the software support period for Apple TV devices launched since the 2012 model, which is also referred to as Apple TV (3rd Generation). The 2012 model received software updates for nearly ten years, whereas the 2015 Apple TV HD and the first-generation Apple TV 4K, which came out in 2017, got their last software update in 2026 . Apple is currently supporting only two Apple TV models: the 2nd and 3rd generations of the Apple TV 4K, both of which received the tvOS 27 update in September 2026. While the second-generation model was launched in 2021, the third-generation model came in 2022. The company hasn't released a newer model since then. If the support period for the last few generations of Apple TV models is any indication, the newer Apple TV 4K models are expected to see updates until around 2030-2031, if not longer. However, exactly which features reach these models in future updates will depend on their hardware, particularly as the company focuses on Apple Intelligence, which can't run on older chips. Still, if you're in the market for a streaming media player and are considering the Apple TV 4K (2022), the device won't become obsolete anytime soon. But if you want software updates for a decade or so, you might want to wait for the next-generation Apple TV model, which is expected to launch in October at the company's Welcome Home event. Similarly, if you already own the 2021 or 2022 model, there is no rush to upgrade or switch to a different media streamer if you are enjoying your Apple TV device. It's important to remember that even after Apple stops releasing new tvOS updates for your hardware, it won't become unusable. You can keep using it as long as you want, probably until it becomes sluggish, a chore to operate, or until your favorite streaming apps stop supporting it.

passages: Hyperliquid recently hit its peak of around $98 on September 23.
Monero reached about $798 on January 14, while Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, set its record at $126,080 on October 6, 2025.
Given these figures, which of these three might reach a new all-time high first?
43% for Monero and 55% for Bitcoin, making it the likeliest candidate.
As of October 17, 2026, Hyperliquid trades around $80, Monero around $558, and Bitcoin around $81,497.
Hyperliquid needs a smaller percentage increase, and its daily buyer-through trading fees and the recent introduction of new trading platforms strengthen its position.
In contrast, Bitcoin would need to rise from about $1.64 trillion to $2.53 trillion to hit a record.
To hit its record, Hyperliquid needs only a 22.9% increase, while Monero needs 42.9% and Bitcoin needs 54.7%.

Hyperliquid ( CRYPTO: HYPE ), Monero ( CRYPTO: XMR ), and Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) stand out among large cryptocurrencies as the closest to a new all-time high , but their distances to those peaks vary significantly. As of October 17, 2026, Hyperliquid trades around $80, Monero around $558, and Bitcoin around $81,497.

Hyperliquid recently hit its peak of around $98 on September 23. Monero reached about $798 on January 14, while Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, set its record at $126,080 on October 6, 2025. Given these figures, which of these three might reach a new all-time high first?
To hit its record, Hyperliquid needs only a 22.9% increase, while Monero needs 42.9% and Bitcoin needs 54.7%. This puts Hyperliquid in the lead based on price distance alone.

Market capitalization, calculated by multiplying the coin’s price by its circulating supply, shows the dollar value needed to reach each record. If Hyperliquid hit its previous peak at its current supply, it would have a market cap of about $21.8 billion, up from $17.7 billion.

For Monero, its all-time high would imply a valuation of around $15 billion, up from the current $10.5 billion. In contrast, Bitcoin would need to rise from about $1.64 trillion to $2.53 trillion to hit a record.

However, supply dilution—when more coins enter circulation—makes it harder for older prices to repeat. Hyperliquid currently has around 222.4 million tokens in circulation out of a total supply of 955.3 million. This means its fully diluted value could reach approximately $93.6 billion at its record price.

Monero, on the other hand, has no maximum supply because of its tail emission, which rewards miners indefinitely. Bitcoin has around 20.1 million coins in circulation with a hard cap of 21 million, so its dilution effect is minimal.

Hyperliquid operates as a crypto exchange, specializing in perpetual futures—contracts that don’t expire and track price movements. The platform spends about 97% to 99% of its trading fees to buy back and burn HYPE tokens, so higher trading volumes generally create consistent buying pressure. As of September 26, about 47.5 million HYPE tokens had been removed from circulation, costing roughly $1.32 billion.

Monero, known for its privacy features that obscure transaction details, needs to maintain its upward momentum. Over the week leading up to October 17, it rose 8.1%, while Bitcoin fell 1.5% and Hyperliquid fell 5.2%.

In the last 30 days, Monero is up 13.5% and is up 85.7% over the past year, driven by broader interest in privacy-focused cryptocurrencies, which also benefited Zcash ( CRYPTO:ZEC ). The sustainability of this interest will greatly affect Monero’s next price move.

Bitcoin’s climb relies on renewed interest from spot ETF buyers. These funds buy and hold Bitcoin directly and trade like stocks. On October 15, cumulative net inflows into these funds totaled about $57 billion, slightly below the $57.8 billion peak recorded on October 6.

The funds attracted about $999 million on September 21 and another $715 million afterward, but volatility has since set in , including a $261.5 million outflow on October 14, followed by only about $5.1 million in inflows.

Hyperliquid faces challenges from scheduled token unlocks, which release team and community tokens and could increase selling pressure. Additionally, when trading activity slows, its buyback mechanism weakens, often during price declines. Moreover, Deribit is introducing over 90 USDC-settled contracts, which could split institutional trading volume across exchanges.

Monero’s primary challenge is liquidity. Many exchanges have delisted privacy coins because of stricter compliance measures, leaving the market thin. This makes Monero’s price susceptible to large swings with small orders. Furthermore, it currently lacks a US spot ETF.

Bitcoin also faces a potential hurdle from index provider MSCI, which will implement new rules in November. These rules will affect companies holding large amounts of digital assets , and Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), which reported holding 846,000 bitcoins as of the second quarter, was flagged as possibly ineligible. Index-driven selling could dampen market sentiment, although companies are removed from the index only after failing the screening process in two consecutive annual filings.

Monero, on the other hand, has no maximum supply because of its tail emission, which rewards miners indefinitely. Bitcoin has around 20.1 million coins in circulation with a hard cap of 21 million, so its dilution effect is minimal.

Hyperliquid operates as a crypto exchange, specializing in perpetual futures—contracts that don't expire and track price movements. The platform spends about 97% to 99% of its trading fees to buy back and burn HYPE tokens, so higher trading volumes generally create consistent buying pressure. As of September 26, about 47.5 million HYPE tokens had been removed from circulation, costing roughly $1.32 billion.

On October 15, Ripple Prime launched swaps on Hyperliquid markets, and on October 16, Pump. fun introduced Hyperliquid-powered perpetual futures. However, despite these events, HYPE rose only 0.8% on Ripple's launch day.

Monero, known for its privacy features that obscure transaction details, needs to maintain its upward momentum. Over the week leading up to October 17, it rose 8.1%, while Bitcoin fell 1.5% and Hyperliquid fell 5.2%.

Bitcoin's climb relies on renewed interest from spot ETF buyers. These funds buy and hold Bitcoin directly and trade like stocks. On October 15, cumulative net inflows into these funds totaled about $57 billion, slightly below the $57.8 billion peak recorded on October 6.

Hyperliquid faces challenges from scheduled token unlocks, which release team and community tokens and could increase selling pressure. Additionally, when trading activity slows, its buyback mechanism weakens, often during price declines. Moreover, Deribit is introducing over 90 USDC-settled contracts, which could split institutional trading volume across exchanges.

Monero's primary challenge is liquidity. Many exchanges have delisted privacy coins because of stricter compliance measures, leaving the market thin. This makes Monero's price susceptible to large swings with small orders. Furthermore, it currently lacks a US spot ETF.

Bitcoin also faces a potential hurdle from index provider MSCI, which will implement new rules in November. These rules will affect companies holding large amounts of digital assets, and Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR ), which reported holding 846,000 bitcoins as of the second quarter, was flagged as possibly ineligible. Index-driven selling could dampen market sentiment, although companies are removed from the index only after failing the screening process in two consecutive annual filings.

Hyperliquid needs a smaller percentage increase, and its daily buyer-through trading fees and the recent introduction of new trading platforms strengthen its position. Crypto traders often call October “ Uptober ” because Bitcoin has historically posted strong gains during this month. However, in 2026, the trend seems to be reversing. As of October 17, Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is trading at $81,497, down from $84,856 on October 1.

So far in October, Bitcoin has experienced fluctuations, reaching a high of $87,249 and a low of $79,676. With just two weeks left in October, traders are left wondering: is Uptober over, or can Bitcoin still capitalize on its historical performance for a green month?

Bitcoin isn’t the only cryptocurrency facing challenges in October. The three major altcoins— Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL )—have all fallen more sharply, each down over 10% since the start of the month.
XRP has seen the biggest drop, down 12.3%. This pattern is typical when traders reduce risk exposure, often starting with smaller coins, while Bitcoin tends to hold up better.

To gauge whether Uptober is over, look at Bitcoin’s performance in previous Octobers. A positive October means Bitcoin’s closing price will be higher than its opening price. Since 2017, there have been two red Octobers, as shown in the table below:

Over the last nine Octobers, Bitcoin has had seven positive months and only two negative ones. 2025 broke a six-year streak of green Octobers, even as Bitcoin hit a record high of $126,296 that month. Currently, Bitcoin is trading about 23.4% lower than one year ago, highlighting how today’s market feels different for investors.
To regain lost ground, Bitcoin would need to rise about 4.1% from its October 17 price of $81,497 to return to its October 1 open of $84,856 . Several factors have driven its decline this month.

First, forced selling has played a significant role. On October 8, when Bitcoin’s price dipped below $81,000, exchanges liquidated $974 million in cryptocurrency positions, including $896 million in long positions. Liquidation occurs when a trader must sell a leveraged position because losses exceed their collateral. Rising oil prices and geopolitical tensions have contributed to the selling pressure.

Second, inflation concerns have weighed heavily. The Consumer Price Index , the government’s main measure of inflation, rose 0.6% in September, with a year-over-year increase of 3.7%. With the Federal Reserve having raised interest rates in September, market sentiment is influenced by anticipation of its next meeting on October 28. As of October 14, futures traders were pricing in a 47% chance of another rate hike.

Third, there has been notable fund selling, particularly from spot Bitcoin ETFs —funds that hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks. These funds saw a total outflow of $487 million on October 7, $244 million the following day, and another $261 million on October 14, before a small inflow of $5 million on October 15. Consequently, cumulative net inflows fell from approximately $57.6 billion on October 1 to $56.96 billion by October 15. This contrasts sharply with September, when these funds saw a significant inflow of $999 million on September 21 alone.

While Uptober isn’t officially over, Bitcoin’s chances of finishing the month positively look slim. The seven previous green Octobers since 2017 offer hope, but those months often occurred in more favorable market conditions. For Bitcoin to close October positively, it needs to stay above its low of $79,676, ETF flows must shift back to steady inflows, and the Fed must decide against raising rates on October 28.

Even if these conditions align, Bitcoin will have only three days after the Fed meeting to push past its October 1 level of $84,856. Michael Saylor, executive chairman of Strategy ( NASDAQ:MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), commented on October 13, saying, “I think we hit the bottom slightly below $60,000,” but Bitcoin still requires a significant increase to end the month higher. If Bitcoin closes below $84,856 on October 31, it will mark back-to-back red Octobers for the first time since at least 2017.

Conversely, if October begins weakly, those expectations can prompt quick selling, which may push prices down further. Over the past week, every major cryptocurrency has fallen, with Bitcoin down 3%. Moreover, no specific event or trigger in October guarantees strong Bitcoin performance.

With just two weeks left in October, traders are left wondering: is Uptober over, or can Bitcoin still capitalize on its historical performance for a green month? Bitcoin isn’t the only cryptocurrency facing challenges in October. The three major altcoins— Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL )—have all fallen more sharply, each down over 10% since the start of the month. Currently, Bitcoin is trading about 23.4% lower than one year ago, highlighting how today’s market feels different for investors. To regain lost ground, Bitcoin would need to rise about 4.1% from its October 17 price of $81,497 to return to its October 1 open of $84,856 . Several factors have driven its decline this month. First, forced selling has played a significant role. On October 8, when Bitcoin’s price dipped below $81,000, exchanges liquidated $974 million in cryptocurrency positions, including $896 million in long positions. Liquidation occurs when a trader must sell a leveraged position because losses exceed their collateral. Rising oil prices and geopolitical tensions have contributed to the selling pressure. Second, inflation concerns have weighed heavily. The Consumer Price Index , the government’s main measure of inflation, rose 0.6% in September, with a year-over-year increase of 3.7%. With the Federal Reserve having raised interest rates in September, market sentiment is influenced by anticipation of its next meeting on October 28. As of October 14, futures traders were pricing in a 47% chance of another rate hike. Third, there has been notable fund selling, particularly from spot Bitcoin ETFs —funds that hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks. These funds saw a total outflow of $487 million on October 7, $244 million the following day, and another $261 million on October 14, before a small inflow of $5 million on October 15. Consequently, cumulative net inflows fell from approximately $57.6 billion on October 1 to $56.96 billion by October 15. This contrasts sharply with September, when these funds saw a significant inflow of $999 million on September 21 alone. While Uptober isn’t officially over, Bitcoin’s chances of finishing the month positively look slim. The seven previous green Octobers since 2017 offer hope, but those months often occurred in more favorable market conditions. To regain lost ground, Bitcoin would need to rise about 4.1% from its October 17 price of $81,497 to return to its October 1 open of $84,856 . Several factors have driven its decline this month.

This contrasts sharply with September, when these funds saw a significant inflow of $999 million on September 21 alone.

While Uptober isn’t officially over, Bitcoin’s chances of finishing the month positively look slim. Crypto traders often call October “ Uptober ” because Bitcoin has historically posted strong gains during this month.
However, in 2026, the trend seems to be reversing.
As of October 17, Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is trading at $81,497, down from $84,856 on October 1.
So far in October, Bitcoin has experienced fluctuations, reaching a high of $87,249 and a low of $79,676.
With just two weeks left in October, traders are left wondering: is Uptober over, or can Bitcoin still capitalize on its historical performance for a green month?
In mid-November 2025, investors pulled nearly $900 million from spot Bitcoin ETFs in a single day, marking the second-largest withdrawal since the funds launched in January 2024.
The rally started in early January and peaked at $126,000 on October 6, but the Bitcoin price erased all those gains over the…
These funds saw a total outflow of $487 million on October 7, $244 million the following day, and another $261 million on October 14, before a small inflow of $5 million on October 15.
To gauge whether Uptober is over, look at Bitcoin’s performance in previous Octobers.
A positive October means Bitcoin’s closing price will be higher than its opening price.
Over the last nine Octobers, Bitcoin has had seven positive months and only two negative ones.
2025 broke a six-year streak of green Octobers, even as Bitcoin hit a record high of $126,296 that month.
While Uptober isn’t officially over, Bitcoin’s chances of finishing the month positively look slim.

Michael Saylor, executive chairman of Strategy ( NASDAQ:MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), commented on October 13, saying, “I think we hit the bottom slightly below $60,000,” but Bitcoin still requires a significant increase to end the month higher.
Bitcoin isn’t the only cryptocurrency facing challenges in October.
On October 8, when Bitcoin’s price dipped below $81,000, exchanges liquidated $974 million in cryptocurrency positions, including $896 million in long positions.
Bitcoin's famous October winning streak has survived over a decade of market chaos, but last year it finally cracked.
Bitcoin ETFs command nearly $52 billion in cumulative inflows, yet two smaller rivals have quietly outpaced it in percentage growth this year.

Peter Schiff, an economist known for advocating gold and criticizing Bitcoin, is back with his familiar advice: he tells Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) investors to switch.
In a post on X circulating on October 16, 2026, he urged, “SELL your Bitcoin before the bottom drops out of the market and buy gold.”
But his latest warning lands at a moment when Bitcoin sits 35% below its all-time high…
McGlone has reiterated his Bitcoin $10,000 prediction multiple…
Schiff has suggested selling Bitcoin multiple times, but many of those predictions haven’t aged well.
Gold, although it has fared slightly better in 2026, has still fallen 4.6% year-to-date and 21.3% from its February close due to rising interest rates.
If Schiff’s sell call proves right, Bitcoin would need to close below the late-June low of $57,717 and then fall below $50,000.
If Bitcoin stays above $57,717 into 2027, this prediction could join his earlier misses.

While Schiff is technically right that gold has lost less value than Bitcoin in 2026, gold peaked earlier in the year, making its decline look more dramatic.
Higher interest rates and rising inflation have negatively affected both Bitcoin and gold.
In September, U.S. inflation increased to 3.7% from 3.4% in August, and the Federal Reserve raised interest rates on September 16.
Because neither gold nor Bitcoin pays interest, rising rates make them less appealing than interest-bearing assets.

The MicroStrategy chairman's comments come as Deutsche Bank reportedly positions itself to offer Bitcoin-backed lending once it secures the necessary internal and regulatory sign-offs.

Michael Saylor, Chairman of MicroStrategy, wrote that with the CLARITY Act stalling in Congress, he expects the SEC and CFTC to advance crypto rules under existing law, and for banks to expand Bitcoin custody and loans against it as a result.
If Saylor's prediction holds, it could accelerate Bitcoin's integration into traditional finance and reshape how banks assess digital-asset-backed loans.
With Bitcoin trading near $76,000 today, how can banks currently lend against Bitcoin, and would there be any ripple effect on Bitcoin's price?
OCC interpretive letters are not statute but guidance, and a future administration or a court challenge can revoke them without a single vote in Congress.
If the price falls far enough to breach that cushion, the bank can require more collateral or repayment, and sell the Bitcoin outright if the borrower can't meet the call.
Deutsche Bank announced this week that it plans to launch regulated custody for Bitcoin, Ethereum and select stablecoins for institutional and corporate clients by the end of 2026.

A holder who needs cash can borrow against Bitcoin at a bank rate instead of triggering a taxable sale, which keeps that Bitcoin out of active circulation while still meeting the holder's liquidity needs.
Saylor's Strategy has leaned on this logic for years through its preferred-stock products, and regulated bank lending would extend the same idea to a much wider set of institutional holders.

Deutsche Bank's custody launch is awaiting approval, which depends on clearance from BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, under the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation.
Deutsche Bank already holds a German crypto-custody authorization, but the specific service it announced still needs BaFin's sign-off before it goes live.

Regulated banks are likely to run more conservative loan-to-value ratios than those platforms did, but the underlying mechanism, forced selling triggered by falling prices, doesn't disappear just because a bank is the lender.
Neither side of that risk changes what bank lending ultimately does to Bitcoin's position in the financial system.

Several large U.S. banks have since launched programs accepting Bitcoin and Ethereum as loan collateral, and New York's adoption of updated Uniform Commercial Code rules in June gave lenders a clearer legal path to perfect a security interest in digital-asset collateral, the same kind of legal mechanism banks use for stocks and bonds.
The real gate for bank Bitcoin loans is Basel Committee and Fed capital treatment rules, which determine how much equity must sit behind each dollar of Bitcoin collateral.

Michael Saylor, Chairman of MicroStrategy, wrote that with the CLARITY Act stalling in Congress, he expects the SEC and CFTC to advance crypto rules under existing law, and for banks to expand Bitcoin custody and loans against it as a result. Unlike the other tokens the CLARITY Act was meant to classify, Bitcoin already has a settled legal status as a CFTC-regulated commodity with SEC-approved spot ETFs, so its path into bank lending doesn't depend on Congress resolving anything new. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has also issued a series of interpretive letters since March 2025 confirming that national banks may custody crypto assets, execute trades at customer direction, and outsource those services to sub-custodians, all under authority the agency already had. (sponsor) Several large U.S. banks have since launched programs accepting Bitcoin and Ethereum as loan collateral, and New York's adoption of updated Uniform Commercial Code rules in June gave lenders a clearer legal path to perfect a security interest in digital-asset collateral, the same kind of legal mechanism banks use for stocks and bonds. None of that ground is as solid as it looks, which is where Saylor's argument runs thin. OCC interpretive letters are not statute but guidance, and a future administration or a court challenge can revoke them without a single vote in Congress. However, the CLARITY Act, if passed by Congress, would lock Bitcoin's commodity status and banks' authority to lend against it into law in a way no agency letter can. Deutsche Bank announced this week that it plans to launch regulated custody for Bitcoin, Ethereum and select stablecoins for institutional and corporate clients by the end of 2026. The bank, which reported $2.217 trillion in assets under management as of June 30, has spent nearly a decade building toward this, including a 2023 partnership with Swiss custody firm Taurus. So far, that plan covers only custody, not lending. Deutsche Bank's custody launch is awaiting approval, which depends on clearance from BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, under the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation. MiCA's transition period ended on July 1, and any firm offering crypto custody or administration in the EU now needs a license under that framework. Deutsche Bank already holds a German crypto-custody authorization, but the specific service it announced still needs BaFin's sign-off before it goes live. That sign-off matters beyond custody alone, since it's also the first piece any bank needs before it can lend against Bitcoin at all, and the bank has to hold the collateral to secure the loan. Typically, a borrower would post Bitcoin with the bank's custody arm, and the bank would lend a portion of its value, well under 100%, given how much Bitcoin's price moves. If the price falls far enough to breach that cushion, the bank can require more collateral or repayment, and sell the Bitcoin outright if the borrower can't meet the call. Bitcoin-backed lending gives large holders a reason to keep coins instead of selling them. A holder who needs cash can borrow against Bitcoin at a bank rate instead of triggering a taxable sale, which keeps that Bitcoin out of active circulation while still meeting the holder's liquidity needs. Saylor's Strategy has leaned on this logic for years through its preferred-stock products, and regulated bank lending would extend the same idea to a much wider set of institutional holders. That same structure works in reverse once prices turn. If Bitcoin's price drops sharply, banks holding it as collateral issue margin calls, and borrowers who can't post more collateral get force-sold. That's roughly what happened across unregulated crypto lenders in 2022, when Celsius, BlockFi, and Voyager collapsed under exactly this kind of leverage. Regulated banks are likely to run more conservative loan-to-value ratios than those platforms did, but the underlying mechanism, forced selling triggered by falling prices, doesn't disappear just because a bank is the lender. Neither side of that risk changes what bank lending ultimately does to Bitcoin's position in the financial system. It pulls Bitcoin further into the same credit system that already runs on stocks, bonds and real estate, treating it as a recognized form of collateral instead of an asset banks mostly avoid. However, that shift is still early, as Deutsche Bank hasn't launched custody yet, let alone lending, and most of the U.S. programs Saylor pointed to remain small relative to Bitcoin's total market. The structural change Saylor described is real, but it will unfold gradually, with banks like Deutsche Bank clearing one regulatory approval at a time, not through a single announcement that moves Bitcoin's price overnight.
