coreStoryFacts.text: Michael Saylor believes Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) lending is coming to mainstream banking with or without new legislation from Congress.
The MicroStrategy chairman's comments come as Deutsche Bank reportedly positions itself to offer Bitcoin-backed lending once it secures the necessary internal and regulatory sign-offs.

Michael Saylor, Chairman of MicroStrategy, wrote that with the CLARITY Act stalling in Congress, he expects the SEC and CFTC to advance crypto rules under existing law, and for banks to expand Bitcoin custody and loans against it as a result.
If Saylor's prediction holds, it could accelerate Bitcoin's integration into traditional finance and reshape how banks assess digital-asset-backed loans.
With Bitcoin trading near $76,000 today, how can banks currently lend against Bitcoin, and would there be any ripple effect on Bitcoin's price?
OCC interpretive letters are not statute but guidance, and a future administration or a court challenge can revoke them without a single vote in Congress.
If the price falls far enough to breach that cushion, the bank can require more collateral or repayment, and sell the Bitcoin outright if the borrower can't meet the call.
Deutsche Bank announced this week that it plans to launch regulated custody for Bitcoin, Ethereum and select stablecoins for institutional and corporate clients by the end of 2026.

A holder who needs cash can borrow against Bitcoin at a bank rate instead of triggering a taxable sale, which keeps that Bitcoin out of active circulation while still meeting the holder's liquidity needs.
Saylor's Strategy has leaned on this logic for years through its preferred-stock products, and regulated bank lending would extend the same idea to a much wider set of institutional holders.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Deutsche Bank's custody launch is awaiting approval, which depends on clearance from BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, under the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation.
Deutsche Bank already holds a German crypto-custody authorization, but the specific service it announced still needs BaFin's sign-off before it goes live.

Regulated banks are likely to run more conservative loan-to-value ratios than those platforms did, but the underlying mechanism, forced selling triggered by falling prices, doesn't disappear just because a bank is the lender.
Neither side of that risk changes what bank lending ultimately does to Bitcoin's position in the financial system.

Several large U.S. banks have since launched programs accepting Bitcoin and Ethereum as loan collateral, and New York's adoption of updated Uniform Commercial Code rules in June gave lenders a clearer legal path to perfect a security interest in digital-asset collateral, the same kind of legal mechanism banks use for stocks and bonds.
The real gate for bank Bitcoin loans is Basel Committee and Fed capital treatment rules, which determine how much equity must sit behind each dollar of Bitcoin collateral.
More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it.
Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders.

The MicroStrategy chairman's comments come as Deutsche Bank reportedly positions itself to offer Bitcoin-backed lending once it secures the necessary internal and regulatory sign-offs.

Michael Saylor, Chairman of MicroStrategy, wrote that with the CLARITY Act stalling in Congress, he expects the SEC and CFTC to advance crypto rules under existing law, and for banks to expand Bitcoin custody and loans against it as a result.
If Saylor's prediction holds, it could accelerate Bitcoin's integration into traditional finance and reshape how banks assess digital-asset-backed loans.
With Bitcoin trading near $76,000 today, how can banks currently lend against Bitcoin, and would there be any ripple effect on Bitcoin's price?
OCC interpretive letters are not statute but guidance, and a future administration or a court challenge can revoke them without a single vote in Congress.
If the price falls far enough to breach that cushion, the bank can require more collateral or repayment, and sell the Bitcoin outright if the borrower can't meet the call.
Deutsche Bank announced this week that it plans to launch regulated custody for Bitcoin, Ethereum and select stablecoins for institutional and corporate clients by the end of 2026.

A holder who needs cash can borrow against Bitcoin at a bank rate instead of triggering a taxable sale, which keeps that Bitcoin out of active circulation while still meeting the holder's liquidity needs.
Saylor's Strategy has leaned on this logic for years through its preferred-stock products, and regulated bank lending would extend the same idea to a much wider set of institutional holders.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Deutsche Bank's custody launch is awaiting approval, which depends on clearance from BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, under the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation.
Deutsche Bank already holds a German crypto-custody authorization, but the specific service it announced still needs BaFin's sign-off before it goes live.

Regulated banks are likely to run more conservative loan-to-value ratios than those platforms did, but the underlying mechanism, forced selling triggered by falling prices, doesn't disappear just because a bank is the lender.
Neither side of that risk changes what bank lending ultimately does to Bitcoin's position in the financial system.

Several large U.S. banks have since launched programs accepting Bitcoin and Ethereum as loan collateral, and New York's adoption of updated Uniform Commercial Code rules in June gave lenders a clearer legal path to perfect a security interest in digital-asset collateral, the same kind of legal mechanism banks use for stocks and bonds.
The real gate for bank Bitcoin loans is Basel Committee and Fed capital treatment rules, which determine how much equity must sit behind each dollar of Bitcoin collateral.
More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it.
Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank’s crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027.
If Citi or State Street announces a dated go-live for Bitcoin custody before December 31, the follow-the-leader view gains hard evidence.
In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany.
Additional services, such as stablecoin offerings, tokenized deposits (which record traditional bank deposits on a blockchain), and digital bonds, will follow, but no specific dates have been set.
Custody banks typically charge a small annual fee, so this business model will be sustainable primarily if clients entrust them with significant assets.
It became the first of the eight U.S. banks deemed systemically important—banks whose failure could impact the wider economy—to safely hold digital currencies.
Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase.
Bank regulators have flipped their crypto stance with every new president since 2017, and Wall Street is already pricing in rules that the next administration could erase overnight.
The fate of Bitcoin's banking access…
By holding these keys, a bank allows institutions like pension funds or corporate treasuries to own cryptocurrency without needing to handle the keys themselves .
Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved.

The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market.

With Bitcoin trading near $76,000 today, how can banks currently lend against Bitcoin, and would there be any ripple effect on Bitcoin's price? Michael Saylor, Chairman of MicroStrategy, wrote that with the CLARITY Act stalling in Congress, he expects the SEC and CFTC to advance crypto rules under existing law, and for banks to expand Bitcoin custody and loans against it as a result. Unlike the other tokens the CLARITY Act was meant to classify, Bitcoin already has a settled legal status as a CFTC-regulated commodity with SEC-approved spot ETFs, so its path into bank lending doesn't depend on Congress resolving anything new. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has also issued a series of interpretive letters since March 2025 confirming that national banks may custody crypto assets, execute trades at customer direction, and outsource those services to sub-custodians, all under authority the agency already had. (sponsor) Several large U.S. banks have since launched programs accepting Bitcoin and Ethereum as loan collateral, and New York's adoption of updated Uniform Commercial Code rules in June gave lenders a clearer legal path to perfect a security interest in digital-asset collateral, the same kind of legal mechanism banks use for stocks and bonds. None of that ground is as solid as it looks, which is where Saylor's argument runs thin. OCC interpretive letters are not statute but guidance, and a future administration or a court challenge can revoke them without a single vote in Congress. However, the CLARITY Act, if passed by Congress, would lock Bitcoin's commodity status and banks' authority to lend against it into law in a way no agency letter can. Deutsche Bank announced this week that it plans to launch regulated custody for Bitcoin, Ethereum and select stablecoins for institutional and corporate clients by the end of 2026. The bank, which reported $2.217 trillion in assets under management as of June 30, has spent nearly a decade building toward this, including a 2023 partnership with Swiss custody firm Taurus. So far, that plan covers only custody, not lending. Deutsche Bank's custody launch is awaiting approval, which depends on clearance from BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, under the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation. MiCA's transition period ended on July 1, and any firm offering crypto custody or administration in the EU now needs a license under that framework. Deutsche Bank already holds a German crypto-custody authorization, but the specific service it announced still needs BaFin's sign-off before it goes live. That sign-off matters beyond custody alone, since it's also the first piece any bank needs before it can lend against Bitcoin at all, and the bank has to hold the collateral to secure the loan. Typically, a borrower would post Bitcoin with the bank's custody arm, and the bank would lend a portion of its value, well under 100%, given how much Bitcoin's price moves. If the price falls far enough to breach that cushion, the bank can require more collateral or repayment, and sell the Bitcoin outright if the borrower can't meet the call. Bitcoin-backed lending gives large holders a reason to keep coins instead of selling them. A holder who needs cash can borrow against Bitcoin at a bank rate instead of triggering a taxable sale, which keeps that Bitcoin out of active circulation while still meeting the holder's liquidity needs. Saylor's Strategy has leaned on this logic for years through its preferred-stock products, and regulated bank lending would extend the same idea to a much wider set of institutional holders. That same structure works in reverse once prices turn. If Bitcoin's price drops sharply, banks holding it as collateral issue margin calls, and borrowers who can't post more collateral get force-sold. That's roughly what happened across unregulated crypto lenders in 2022, when Celsius, BlockFi, and Voyager collapsed under exactly this kind of leverage. Regulated banks are likely to run more conservative loan-to-value ratios than those platforms did, but the underlying mechanism, forced selling triggered by falling prices, doesn't disappear just because a bank is the lender. Neither side of that risk changes what bank lending ultimately does to Bitcoin's position in the financial system. It pulls Bitcoin further into the same credit system that already runs on stocks, bonds and real estate, treating it as a recognized form of collateral instead of an asset banks mostly avoid. However, that shift is still early, as Deutsche Bank hasn't launched custody yet, let alone lending, and most of the U.S. programs Saylor pointed to remain small relative to Bitcoin's total market. The structural change Saylor described is real, but it will unfold gradually, with banks like Deutsche Bank clearing one regulatory approval at a time, not through a single announcement that moves Bitcoin's price overnight. Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) has dropped 10.2% since October 1, 2026, but social media sentiment remains optimistic. According to Santiment, a prominent crypto analytics firm that monitors social media discussions and blockchain activities, 59.1% of posts about ETH over the latest 24 hours are positive.

Ethereum started October at $2,705 and is now trading around $2,428 as of October 17, down 0.8% in the last 24 hours. The cryptocurrency peaked at $2,777 on October 2 before plummeting to a low of $2,313 on October 15, a day when ETH led the market in liquidations , the forced closures of leveraged trades that ran out of collateral.
While sentiment appears hopeful, the persistent decline raises one question. Is the crowd too early on Ethereum?

Santiment’s analysis shows that 59.1% of ETH posts are bullish, compared with 57.9% for Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ). Furthermore, Santiment’s intensity metric—which measures how strongly posts express sentiment—ranks ETH at 54.1%, while Bitcoin scores 52.2%. This indicates that, despite ETH’s weaker price, its community remains more optimistic than Bitcoin’s.
In the past month, ETH has lost 1.1%, while Bitcoin has gained 6.8%. Additionally, for 2026, ETH is down 18.4% compared to Bitcoin’s 6.8% decline.
Sentiment readings reflect what people say, not necessarily what they do with their assets. A participant can express bullish sentiment one day and sell their ETH the next.

Santiment has consistently viewed crowd optimism during a downturn as a potential warning, whereas fear can indicate more favorable entry points. When most holders remain hopeful for a rebound, it often suggests that those likely to panic and sell have not yet exited their positions, potentially leading to further declines.

Much of the current optimism may stem from Ethereum’s summer rally, as ETH is still up 26.7% over 60 days from $1,917 on August 18. This is likely fresh in many holders’ minds, overshadowing the current downturn.

In contrast to bullish sentiment on social media, fund investors appear to be withdrawing. The U.S. spot Ether ETFs, which trade on U.S. stock exchanges and hold ETH directly, experienced net outflows on five out of six trading days from October 8 to 15, as reported by SoSoValue. The most significant outflow occurred on October 14, with $130 million exiting the funds, followed by another $60 million on October 15.

A brief inflow on October 13 lasted only a day . The cumulative net inflow—the total amount invested in the funds since their launch minus withdrawals—dropped from $13.3 billion on October 8 to $13.0 billion on October 15, reflecting a decrease of approximately $306 million. Total ETF assets stood at $15.3 billion on October 15.

Interactive Brokers, one of the largest online brokers in the U.S., has enabled clients to stake Ethereum , which involves locking ETH to help secure the network in exchange for rewards. This new option might attract new buyers eventually, but the ETF flows have not yet shown any sign of recovery.

It appears that the crowd might indeed be too early. Optimistic voices in the community contrast sharply with the outflow of funds, and historical trends suggest financial actions usually carry more weight than social sentiment. Santiment’s framework also suggests current Ethereum sentiment could be a warning sign; those buying solely on this mood may be entering ahead of further selling pressure.

For the crowd’s optimism to prove correct, ETF flows would need to turn positive for several sessions, nudging cumulative net inflow back above $13.3 billion. ETH would also need to close above $2,705 to target the $2,777 high. If negative flows persist and ETH dips below its $2,313 low, sentiment may shift from hope to fear, which, according to Santiment, could offer a more advantageous entry point for buyers.

passages: Crude oil has crossed the $ 100-per-barrel mark for the first time since September, sparking curiosity among Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) holders who have seen $100 oil before.
U.S. crude reached $102 a barrel on October 14, 2026—its highest price since mid-September—while Brent crude, the global oil standard, climbed above $106.
Interestingly, Bitcoin reacted to rising oil prices in September.
It closed at $81,264 on September 3, when WTI was around $93 per barrel, but then fell 7% to $75,584 on September 15, coinciding with oil's peak.
During that particular trading session, Bitcoin dipped to as low as $74,888.
Despite a minor cooling off afterward, Bitcoin held most of its gains, closing at $84,849 on October 1, while WTI hovered just below $100.
If history is any guide, Bitcoin's next upward movement may hinge on when oil prices begin to decline again.
The previous trend suggests yes, but the downturn lasted only as long as the oil-price spike.
Bitcoin is currently trading at $81,497, while WTI is around $102 and Brent is above $106.
Although Bitcoin has gained 26.1% over the past 60 days, it remains down 6.8% for 2026.
Notably, Bitcoin also traded through a similar spike in crude oil in September, which could hint at similar movements in the current landscape.
News from the Strait of Hormuz could influence Bitcoin as much as any crypto-related headlines in the coming weeks.
Investors should watch Bitcoin's September 17 close of $76,349.
If oil stays above $100 and Bitcoin closes below that threshold, Bitcoin might repeat its September decline and revisit the $74,888 low from that time.

As oil prices retreated the next day, Bitcoin bounced back to close at $80,875 on September 18, as WTI eased to about $101.
By September 21, when WTI fell to $97, Bitcoin hit an intraday high of $87,397, marking its best performance of that month.
Nevertheless, the relationship between oil and Bitcoin can also diverge.
Some investors turn to Bitcoin as an inflation hedge because of its fixed supply.
A prolonged spike in oil prices that amplifies costs could eventually attract new buyers to Bitcoin.
Investors often shy away from volatile assets, and during these times, Bitcoin frequently trades in tandem with tech stocks.
WTI crude hit $102, mirroring a September spike that sent Bitcoin down 7% before a sharp 16% rebound once oil cooled.
High oil prices fuel inflation and crush risk appetite, historically dragging Bitcoin lower alongside tech stocks until crude retreats.
When crude becomes expensive, it raises costs for gasoline, shipping, and nearly everything that requires transportation, thereby exerting inflationary pressure.

facts.text: Crude oil has crossed the $ 100-per-barrel mark for the first time since September, sparking curiosity among Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) holders who have seen $100 oil before.
U.S. crude reached $102 a barrel on October 14, 2026—its highest price since mid-September—while Brent crude, the global oil standard, climbed above $106.
Interestingly, Bitcoin reacted to rising oil prices in September.
It closed at $81,264 on September 3, when WTI was around $93 per barrel, but then fell 7% to $75,584 on September 15, coinciding with oil's peak.
During that particular trading session, Bitcoin dipped to as low as $74,888.
Despite a minor cooling off afterward, Bitcoin held most of its gains, closing at $84,849 on October 1, while WTI hovered just below $100.
If history is any guide, Bitcoin's next upward movement may hinge on when oil prices begin to decline again.
The previous trend suggests yes, but the downturn lasted only as long as the oil-price spike.
Bitcoin is currently trading at $81,497, while WTI is around $102 and Brent is above $106.
Although Bitcoin has gained 26.1% over the past 60 days, it remains down 6.8% for 2026.
Notably, Bitcoin also traded through a similar spike in crude oil in September, which could hint at similar movements in the current landscape.
News from the Strait of Hormuz could influence Bitcoin as much as any crypto-related headlines in the coming weeks.
Investors should watch Bitcoin's September 17 close of $76,349.
If oil stays above $100 and Bitcoin closes below that threshold, Bitcoin might repeat its September decline and revisit the $74,888 low from that time.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
As oil prices retreated the next day, Bitcoin bounced back to close at $80,875 on September 18, as WTI eased to about $101.
By September 21, when WTI fell to $97, Bitcoin hit an intraday high of $87,397, marking its best performance of that month.
Nevertheless, the relationship between oil and Bitcoin can also diverge.
Some investors turn to Bitcoin as an inflation hedge because of its fixed supply.
A prolonged spike in oil prices that amplifies costs could eventually attract new buyers to Bitcoin.
Investors often shy away from volatile assets, and during these times, Bitcoin frequently trades in tandem with tech stocks.

Bitcoin trades at $81,497, down 1.5% over the previous week but still up 6.8% over the last month. Notably, Bitcoin also traded through a similar spike in crude oil in September, which could hint at similar movements in the current landscape.

In addition, Ukraine has vowed to continue striking Russian refineries. The Strait of Hormuz, lying between Iran and Oman, is crucial since a significant portion of the world’s oil passes through it.

As these tensions persisted into mid-October, oil prices surged. For instance, on October 14, crude prices jumped significantly following attacks in Saudi Arabia and new strategies launched by Iran against tankers. By October 16, Brent oil continued to climb as regional pressure mounted.

Within a week, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil posted a nearly $7 increase, marking a 7.3% rise. According to federal data, WTI peaked at $107 on September 15, its highest level since at least July, but then fell roughly 20% to $85 by September 25 before starting to climb again.

passages: At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did.

extraction.body: Apple’s App Store rules now more explicitly ban so-called “nudify” apps that generate intimate images of people without their consent using AI tools. The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors. Apple didn’t pull X or Grok from the App Store, though it told senators that it threatened to yank Grok. At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did. As part of updates announced Friday, Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps. Developers who “fail to implement adequate safeguards” or “don’t remedy violations after notice” may be removed from the App Store. Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved. Apple’s rules also more clearly spell out that any apps that “facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children” will be pulled from the App Store and “blocked from alternative distribution.”

extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. sources.title: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
passages: Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content.

The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income.
Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs.
I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer.
Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs.

Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions.
“Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.
To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once.
Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious.

“I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board.
There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place.
For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions.

Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.

extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

sources.title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
passages: Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors.
Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images.

sources.title: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
passages: Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5.
It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI.
In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands.
Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures.
Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs.
Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly.

That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon , among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes.

extraction.body: At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote. Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway . Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion. "Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement. The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio. For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the " SaaSpocalypse ." Shares of Intuit , HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro , once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion. "You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore." Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus . Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo , AOL and Eventbrite in 2025. The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07. Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price. Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions. Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied." "They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020. Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years." As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar. "Unfortunately, a lot of my friends in that game are stuck," Mehta said. "Investors want out but there are no buyers. Anything pre-ChatGPT is legacy now." Lloyd Walmsley, an analyst at Mizuho, said Bending Spoons' model is distinct from the older buyout approach. "I think there aren't a lot of people that do what these guys do in terms of the depth of operations and the willingness to make substantial product changes," Walmsley said in an interview. "It's not typical of traditional private equity firms to make anywhere near this level of change." For customers of the companies that Bending Spoons buys, sudden price hikes can follow. In April 2023, months after the Evernote acquisition, Bending Spoons lifted the annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70. Later, the company changed its offerings, charging $100 for its so-called starter plan and $250 for "Evernote Advanced," compared to the $170 it had been charging for the pro plan. "My first reaction was like, Oh man, I guess I have to switch to OneNote," said Walmsley, referring to Microsoft's notetaking app. But he said he stuck with Evernote. "They're really savvy at finding these things that they provide a lot of value, and the switching costs are really high," Walmsley said. "The price isn't that high relative to the switching cost." Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway .

Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion.

"Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement.

The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio.

With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the " SaaSpocalypse ."

Shares of Intuit , HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro , once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion.

A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus .

Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price.

extraction.body: At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote. Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway . Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion. "Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement. The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio. For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the " SaaSpocalypse ." Shares of Intuit , HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro , once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion. "You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore." Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus . Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo , AOL and Eventbrite in 2025. The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07. Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price. Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions. Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied." "They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020. Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years." As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar. "Unfortunately, a lot of my friends in that game are stuck," Mehta said. "Investors want out but there are no buyers. Anything pre-ChatGPT is legacy now." Lloyd Walmsley, an analyst at Mizuho, said Bending Spoons' model is distinct from the older buyout approach. "I think there aren't a lot of people that do what these guys do in terms of the depth of operations and the willingness to make substantial product changes," Walmsley said in an interview. "It's not typical of traditional private equity firms to make anywhere near this level of change." For customers of the companies that Bending Spoons buys, sudden price hikes can follow. In April 2023, months after the Evernote acquisition, Bending Spoons lifted the annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70. Later, the company changed its offerings, charging $100 for its so-called starter plan and $250 for "Evernote Advanced," compared to the $170 it had been charging for the pro plan. "My first reaction was like, Oh man, I guess I have to switch to OneNote," said Walmsley, referring to Microsoft's notetaking app. But he said he stuck with Evernote. "They're really savvy at finding these things that they provide a lot of value, and the switching costs are really high," Walmsley said. "The price isn't that high relative to the switching cost." Bending Spoons uses the profits from its portfolio companies for future growth, the "overwhelming majority" of which comes from doing more deals, Ferrari told CNBC in an interview on Thursday. "There are certain opportunities for improvement we can unlock over the first few years, and then the business will have whatever organic growth is intrinsic in that market," Ferrari said. For Berkshire and its fellow Bending Spoons investors, the bet is still unproven. The products have to remain desirable enough that customers are willing to pay up at a time when AI is squeezing margins across much of the software sector. In its first earnings report as a public company in August, Bending Spoons said revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to over $700 million, with growth almost entirely driven by acquisitions, while net income climbed 171% to $177 million. That was before the Airtable deal had closed and Miro had yet to be announced. In the coming quarters and years, Wall Street will get a clear picture of whether the firm's structure can revive software. On the earnings call in August, an analyst asked whether Airtable represents a long-term shift in the M&A strategy towards enterprise. Ferrari said that about half of Bending Spoons' revenue already comes from professional businesses, largely through Brightcove and Vimeo, which has an enterprise component. The focus on software of late, he said, has more to do with where he's finding value after a hefty selloff. "Most enterprise SaaS businesses were valued at irrationally high levels until somewhat recently," Ferrari said. "We never saw those prices making any sense."

passages: Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee , is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year .

The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.
To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations.
Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted.

Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.
In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking.

The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device .
With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.

Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.
For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite.
Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.

extraction.body: Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee , is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year . The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone. The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device . The Bee Frontier will come in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage, while the $99.99 Bee Eclipse will be offered in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush. Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights. For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite. You could also use the Bee to take lecture notes in class, or to jot down the care plan you discussed with a doctor, among other things. All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory. With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications. Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates. To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations. Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted. Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them. In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking. It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.) With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free. Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more. The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering. All Bee devices come with a companion mobile app, which has also been newly redesigned, plus a new desktop app. The Bee Frontier is available now on Amazon, and the Eclipse will be available soon thereafter. passages: Russia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along the border and it will be non-negotiable in any ⁠future talks with Kyiv, Vladimir Putin has said .

The Russian president, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation ⁠was in response to Ukraine’s ⁠2024-25 incursion into ​Russia’s western Kursk region .
This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments on Friday.
“Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions ⁠for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with ​Ukraine.”
The planned ‌security zone spanned 660km (410 ‌miles) , of which 70% was currently under Russia’s control, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
Peskov did not say how deep it would ‌reach inside Ukraine.
The zone requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it is illegally claiming as its own territory.

Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service had not yet been fully restored , as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels and asked the EU for another €70bn ($79bn/£59bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia, report Jennifer Rankin and Andrew Roth .
Hours earlier Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” after his purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
The attacks came as a new report showed that civilian casualties from Russia’s invasion have climbed steeply.
At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded last month – a total that is 85% higher than in September last year, the report from the UN human rights office in Kyiv said on Friday.
It said intensifying Russian attacks in October already had killed dozens of civilians, including children.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, the UN office head.

As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian, writes Andrew Roth in this analysis .
Two were kiled and 12 more wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, governor Oleh Syniehubov ⁠said.
Further Russian strikes through the evening injured nine, officials said.
A Russian ⁠airstrike on ​Kherson in southern ⁠Ukraine killed one ⁠person ​and ‌injured ‌19 others , the governor ‌said on Saturday.
The person ‌killed was an ​ambulance driver and ⁠a child ​was among the ​injured, ​Oleksandr Prokudin ​said ‌on ​Telegram.

passages: Amazon executive Panos Panay has a message for startup founders: Failure is an inevitable, required part of building a successful product.
Panay emphasized the importance of staying committed to a vision, learning from experience, and moving quickly.

Panay, Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa, and Leo, shared that advice onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, drawing on his own experience at Microsoft, where he spent more than 19 years and weathered one particularly expensive failure.
“I remember being on the front cover of a newspaper, and it just said failure,” Panay said. “But, here’s the thing, it was easy to admit failure.

extraction.body: Amazon executive Panos Panay has a message for startup founders: Failure is an inevitable, required part of building a successful product. Panay, Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa, and Leo, shared that advice onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, drawing on his own experience at Microsoft, where he spent more than 19 years and weathered one particularly expensive failure. “You have to be willing to fail, and actually, not just willing, you actually have to go fail,” Panay said. “If you haven’t failed, you probably haven’t pushed the boundary. It’s literally about harvesting the lessons learned when you fail. You have to be willing to face it, and as you face it, learn from it.” Panay said it’s possible to recover from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, noting that he experienced one himself at Microsoft. He described the launch of the Surface RT, Microsoft’s first tablet computer, as a significant failure during his tenure at the company, one that ultimately led to a nearly $1 billion write-down. “I remember being on the front cover of a newspaper, and it just said failure,” Panay said. “But, here’s the thing, it was easy to admit failure. The trick was, and always is, did you harvest the learnings and understand what happened? All right. What did you learn? Because the failure wasn’t that moment. It was decisions that led up to it two years before that, whether the software wasn’t complete or the inventory was wrong or how we balanced into retail. There were all these steps along the way.” He said founders need to be willing to understand what went wrong, and avoid making excuses, and ultimately accept the failure. “Here’s the other side of it,” he said. “You want to succeed, yeah? You take that failure, but you don’t let go of your vision. That’s it. Surface has done pretty well. You don’t let go of your vision. You don’t break it.” Panay emphasized the importance of staying committed to a vision, learning from experience, and moving quickly. He believes that by embracing failure and learning from setbacks, founders can adapt and make progress faster, even as they encounter new obstacles. “It goes back to the same fundamental, like, have you learned?” he said. “Were you learning along the way? Because if you were learning, then you just change your vector. Usually, it’s not 180 degrees. Usually, it’s just 30 degrees. Take your lessons learned, change a little bit, adapt your vision where it needs to be, and then go. I believe there’s people that hang on too long, but it’s because they haven’t accepted the moment of failure at all.” Aisha is a consumer news reporter at TechCrunch. sources.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps
passages: Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.
With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.
These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to.
To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done.
Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls.
That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.
Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.

“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”
Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.

extraction.body: Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI. Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed. “A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.” By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do. “As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said. Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone. These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them. Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work. “You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. And that’s what we do. That’s critical.” The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI. “Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said. That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. passages: Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.

Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.

“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”

By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do.

“As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said.

Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone.

These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.
Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.

“You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. And that’s what we do. That’s critical.”

The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.

“Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.

“I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. I don’t think that’s the case,” he clarified. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful.”
